title: Security review: audit logs for rollout actions (Dedicated pools)
summary: HarborBank security/GRC team reviewed Redwood’s audit logging and RBAC approach for staged rollouts affecting Dedicated pools (model versions, runtime builds, routing policies, config). Redwood walked through which rollout actions emit audit events, what fields are captured (actor, target pool, old/new stage, reason, override flags, idempotency key), retention/export options, and how customers can evidence change management and least-privilege. HarborBank requested sample event payloads, a definitive retention statement (default vs configurable), and clarification on who can force-promote/hold/abort and how those actions appear in exports/SIEM. Open items include confirming audit export coverage for new event types, and providing a mapping of rollout actions to HarborBank’s change ticket requirements.
topics: Scope of audit events for rollout actions (create/update/promote/abort/hold/force-promote/force-rollback)
RBAC and admin-only overrides; separation of duties
Retention and export (download/API/SIEM), immutability, and tamper evidence
SSO/SAML and identity attribution in audit logs
Evidence required for enterprise approval (sample logs, SOC2, change-management mapping)
Edge cases: API retries/idempotency, missing metrics, and in-flight traffic during rollback
next_steps: Redwood (Kevin/Kaitlyn) to send HarborBank sample audit event payloads for promote/abort/force-promote and a field dictionary (actor, scope, old/new stage, reason, correlation IDs).
Redwood to confirm audit log export pipeline includes new rollout event types and provide current status/ETA if any gaps.
HarborBank to share their minimum retention requirement and SIEM ingestion format constraints (Splunk/CEF/JSON).
Schedule a follow-up 30 min session with HarborBank platform team to walk through RBAC roles and recommended least-privilege setup for rollout operators vs auditors.
action_items: Kevin Osei - Provide sample audit events + export format notes (JSONL) - Due 2025-02-24
Kaitlyn Nguyen - Provide RBAC matrix for rollout actions (who can create/promote/abort/force) and SSO identity mapping - Due 2025-02-25
Paula Mendes - Share rollout action taxonomy and how it maps to change management artifacts (ticket ID / reason) - Due 2025-02-26
Nina Patel - Confirm HarborBank retention + SIEM requirements and whether 1 year is sufficient - Due 2025-02-26
Liam O'Rourke - Coordinate follow-up meeting and send SOC 2 + security package links - Due 2025-02-21
transcript:
HarborBank - Security review: audit logs for rollout actions (Dedicated pools)
Recorded by Fireflies.ai

Date: Thu, Feb 20, 2025
Start time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 47 min

Attendees
Redwood Inference: Liam O'Rourke, Kaitlyn Nguyen, Kevin Osei, Paula Mendes
HarborBank: Nina Patel, Markus Klein, Jenna Wu, Tom Alvarez

---

[00:00] Liam O'Rourke: Alright, I think we’re all here. Thanks everyone for making time. This one is focused on audit logs and permissions around rollout actions, specifically staged rollouts for Dedicated pools.

[00:12] Nina Patel: Yep. Thanks Liam. We have Markus from GRC and Tom from vendor risk. Jenna’s our platform engineer who will actually operate this day to day if we proceed.

[00:23] Liam O'Rourke: Great. On Redwood side I’ve got Kaitlyn, who does authn/authz and security reviews, Kevin who owns audit export and event schema, and Paula who’s PM’ing rollouts and gates.

[00:38] Paula Mendes: Hi everyone.

[00:40] Kevin Osei: Hey.

[00:41] Kaitlyn Nguyen: Hello.

[00:44] Liam O'Rourke: Quick framing: we’ll cover what actions emit audit events, what fields we store and export, RBAC roles and overrides like force-promote and hold, and then retention and evidence you’ll need for internal approval.

[01:02] Markus Klein: Sounds good. And we’ll probably ask about immutability and whether these are user-viewable, exportable, and how long you keep them.

[01:10] Liam O'Rourke: Perfect.

[01:12] Jenna Wu: Also practical question: if I do an action through the UI versus API, do we see the same event? And is there correlation IDs for our change tickets.

[01:21] Kevin Osei: Yep, we can cover that.

[01:24] Tom Alvarez: And whether privileged actions can be restricted. We need separation of duties for production changes.

[01:31] Kaitlyn Nguyen: Understood.

---

[01:35] Liam O'Rourke: Paula, do you want to set the stage on what “rollout actions” mean in this system?

[01:40] Paula Mendes: Sure. When we say staged rollouts for Dedicated pools, we mean a plan with stages, like 1%, 10%, 50%, 100% traffic, or sometimes replica partitions. Each stage can have gates—error rate, p95/p99 latency, saturation, GPU health, OOM, 429s, that kind of stuff—before promotion.

[02:03] Paula Mendes: The “actions” are things like create rollout plan, update the plan (before it’s running), start it, promote from stage N to N+1, put it on hold, abort, and in some cases force-promote or force-rollback if you need an escape hatch.

[02:22] Nina Patel: Great. The escape hatches are the thing that gets our auditors excited, so we want strong controls there.

[02:29] Paula Mendes: Totally fair.

---

[02:32] Kevin Osei: On the audit side, we emit an audit event for every state transition and for any mutating action. So, create, update, promote, abort, hold, resume, and any override action are all events.

[02:48] Kevin Osei: Each event includes: timestamp, actor identity, actor type (user vs service), the account/org, the target resource (Dedicated pool id, rollout plan id), the action name, old state, new state, and a “reason” field which is required for some actions.

[03:07] Markus Klein: Required for which actions?

[03:09] Kevin Osei: Force actions, specifically—force-promote and force-rollback. Also we recommend requiring “reason” for abort, but that one is configurable in policy. In the UI we prompt for it.

[03:23] Jenna Wu: What about regular promote? Like from 10% to 50%.

[03:26] Kevin Osei: For promote we capture stage index change, old_stage and new_stage. Reason is optional but we can support you putting a change ticket ID in there.

[03:37] Tom Alvarez: Do you enforce a change ticket format? Like CAB number?

[03:41] Kevin Osei: Not strictly enforced today, but we can support a regex validation at the org policy layer in enterprise plans. If you need that, we’d flag it as a requirement.

[03:52] Kaitlyn Nguyen: And to be clear, RBAC determines who can call those endpoints. Audit logs are separate—they’re the record.

---

[04:01] Nina Patel: Let’s dig into RBAC. How granular is it? We need something like: operator can promote but cannot force-promote, auditor can view but cannot change, admin can grant permissions.

[04:12] Kaitlyn Nguyen: That aligns with how we structure it. At a high level we have roles, and permissions under them. For Dedicated rollouts, we split permissions into read vs write, and then “override” as a separate privileged permission.

[04:28] Kaitlyn Nguyen: Concretely: 
- dedicated.rollouts.read (view plan, stages, gate evidence)
- dedicated.rollouts.write (create/update plan, start, promote, abort, hold/resume)
- dedicated.rollouts.override (force-promote, force-rollback, bypass gates)
- dedicated.rollouts.admin (manage who has the above)

[04:52] Tom Alvarez: Does “abort” require override?

[04:55] Kaitlyn Nguyen: No, abort is in write. Our philosophy is abort is the safe action.

[05:02] Nina Patel: That’s good.

[05:04] Jenna Wu: What about “update plan while running”? Like editing stages.

[05:08] Paula Mendes: We don’t allow editing stage definitions once a plan is running, except for adding a hold note, or maybe updating a gate threshold in v2. For v1, if you need to change the plan, you abort and create a new one. That’s part of auditability.

[05:26] Markus Klein: That is good for evidence.

---

[05:30] Nina Patel: Identity attribution: we require SSO/SAML. Is the actor in the log our corporate identity, not just an email typed into Redwood?

[05:39] Kaitlyn Nguyen: Yes. When SSO is enabled, the actor field is the user’s Redwood principal which is bound to your IdP subject. In the audit event we store: user_id, email, and the IdP attributes we receive (like the SAML NameID). We also store a session id.

[05:58] Markus Klein: Do you store IP address?

[06:00] Kaitlyn Nguyen: For console actions, yes, we capture source IP and user agent. For API actions, we capture API key id / client id plus source IP. If it’s via a service account, it’ll show service principal.

[06:13] Jenna Wu: Can we create service accounts specifically for automation? Like our pipeline promotes stages?

[06:18] Kaitlyn Nguyen: Yes, service accounts exist. We recommend scoping them to a single account and limiting permissions—usually write without override unless you absolutely need it.

[06:30] Nina Patel: We probably won’t allow override from automation.

[06:33] Kaitlyn Nguyen: That’s a common policy.

---

[06:37] Kevin Osei: One more detail: we add correlation IDs. There’s a request_id for the API call, and an audit_event_id which is unique. For promote and abort we also record an idempotency key if provided.

[06:52] Jenna Wu: Idempotency is important because our tooling retries.

[06:55] Kevin Osei: Exactly. You’ll see something like idempotency_key: “cab-184772-promote-10-to-50” if you want.

[07:03] Markus Klein: That helps for traceability.

---

[07:06] Nina Patel: Retention—what’s the default and what’s max? Our policy is 1 year minimum for admin actions. Some logs are 7 years but that’s usually financial systems; for this, 1 year is likely okay.

[07:20] Kevin Osei: Default retention for audit logs in the console is 400 days for enterprise. For non-enterprise it’s shorter, but for your plan it’s 400 days. We can extend via an add-on, but most regulated customers export to SIEM and treat Redwood as the producer, not the system of record.

[07:41] Tom Alvarez: Do you support continuous export?

[07:43] Kevin Osei: Yes. We have an export API (pull) and a scheduled export job to S3-compatible buckets. Splunk HEC is in beta—depends on your preference.

[07:55] Nina Patel: We’re Splunk.

[07:56] Kevin Osei: Great. We can do JSON lines. CEF is possible but not our default.

[08:04] Markus Klein: Are logs immutable? Like can a Redwood admin delete or edit entries?

[08:10] Kevin Osei: Entries are append-only in our audit store. We don’t provide deletion endpoints. Internal admin access is extremely limited; any internal access is itself audited. For customer-facing exports, you can verify integrity via monotonic IDs and timestamps; we also include a hash chain in our internal pipeline, though we don’t currently expose chain verification as a customer feature.

[08:34] Nina Patel: Ok. We’ll likely rely on export to Splunk for immutability.

---

[08:41] Jenna Wu: Can we talk through what exact events we’ll see for a typical staged rollout? Like create → promote → fail gate → abort.

[08:49] Paula Mendes: Sure. Timeline example:
1) dedicated_pool_rollout_plan.created
2) dedicated_pool_rollout_plan.started (when it goes from draft to running)
3) dedicated_pool_rollout_stage.promoted (stage 0 to stage 1)
4) dedicated_pool_rollout_gate.evaluated events—these are optional as audit events; they’re more telemetry. But we do store gate decisions with evidence.
5) If it fails and you abort: dedicated_pool_rollout_plan.aborted.

[09:18] Jenna Wu: So gate evaluations are not in the audit log?

[09:22] Kevin Osei: Today, the audit log focuses on human/actor actions and state changes. Gate evaluation results are available in the rollout history and can be exported as “rollout evidence” but not every evaluation tick becomes an audit event because it’s high volume.

[09:41] Markus Klein: We’re okay with that if we can export the evidence for why a promotion was allowed.

[09:46] Paula Mendes: Yes, the UI shows gate evidence: query, window, observed value, threshold, pass/fail, and data freshness.

[09:55] Nina Patel: Is that evidence tamper-proof?

[09:59] Paula Mendes: It’s stored as part of the rollout record. You can export it alongside audit events. Kevin, you want to add detail?

[10:06] Kevin Osei: The evidence object is immutable once written for a stage evaluation result. It has a created_at and a source tag (metrics backend). If you export it, it can be stored in your SIEM or GRC system.

---

[10:24] Tom Alvarez: Force-promote. Let’s spend time there. Who can do it, how is it logged, and is the customer notified?

[10:33] Kaitlyn Nguyen: Force-promote is behind dedicated.rollouts.override. We recommend only a small “Break Glass Admin” group. In the UI it shows a warning modal and requires a reason.

[10:47] Kevin Osei: The audit event includes override=true, override_type=force_promote, reason, and also includes the gate status at the time. So you can see “gates failing” and still an override occurred.

[11:03] Markus Klein: Does it include which gates were failing?

[11:06] Kevin Osei: We include a summary list in the event payload (like “latency_p99 failed”, “oom_rate unknown”). The full evidence is in the rollout record export.

[11:18] Nina Patel: That’s important. We need to show that overrides are rare and reviewed.

[11:24] Jenna Wu: And what about “hold”? Is that just a state? Like pause promotions.

[11:28] Paula Mendes: Exactly. Hold means the rollout is paused at current stage. Traffic stays where it is, no auto-promote. You can hold manually or the system can put it into a “held” state if there’s missing data depending on policy.

[11:44] Markus Klein: Wait, system can hold automatically?

[11:47] Paula Mendes: In the current design, missing metrics is fail-closed. So if the system can’t evaluate gates, it blocks promotion. It doesn’t necessarily flip to held automatically, but it will mark the stage as “blocked/unknown”. Some customers want an explicit held state; we’re supporting that.

[12:06] Nina Patel: I like fail-closed for promotion.

[12:09] Jenna Wu: But operationally it can be annoying if telemetry lags.

[12:12] Paula Mendes: Yes, we’ve seen that. The UI calls out staleness and suggests manual verification.

---

[12:22] Liam O'Rourke: Just to connect this to your approval process: typically what we provide is a security package with SOC 2, plus a sample of audit events for the actions you care about, plus documentation of RBAC.

[12:36] Tom Alvarez: We will need a “control mapping” basically. Like: Control 1: least privilege. Control 2: change management. Control 3: audit logging retention.

[12:47] Liam O'Rourke: Understood. We can share a mapping doc, and also show how you can enforce reasons / ticket IDs.

---

[12:57] Markus Klein: Does Redwood support “two-person rule” for force-promote? Like require approval?

[13:04] Kaitlyn Nguyen: We don’t have built-in dual-approval for actions in v1. What we see customers do is: restrict override to a group and require an internal change process. If you need dual control, we can discuss it as roadmap.

[13:18] Nina Patel: For now, we can do that with internal process, but we’d like it on roadmap.

[13:24] Paula Mendes: Noted.

---

[13:26] Jenna Wu: Export formats: will the log include the pool name and the model version? Or just IDs.

[13:34] Kevin Osei: Both. We include IDs as canonical. We also include display_name for the pool and the rollout target artifact: model_version, runtime_build_id, routing_policy_version—whatever the plan is rolling.

[13:50] Jenna Wu: Great.

[13:51] Markus Klein: Any PII in those logs?

[13:54] Kevin Osei: No prompt content, no user data. Actor email is there, and maybe IP address. Resource metadata is operational.

---

[14:03] Nina Patel: I want to verify: are these audit logs separate from regular app logs? We don’t want to search in general logs.

[14:10] Kevin Osei: Correct. Separate “Audit Log” section in Console and separate export API endpoint.

[14:17] Tom Alvarez: Are the logs accessible to tenant admins only?

[14:20] Kaitlyn Nguyen: Controlled by dedicated.rollouts.read and also auditlogs.read. Some companies give auditors auditlogs.read only, without rollouts.read.

[14:33] Jenna Wu: If I have rollouts.read but not auditlogs.read, do I see the history?

[14:37] Kaitlyn Nguyen: You’ll see rollout history for the plan itself (like stage transitions), but the formal audit log view is gated. We can talk through the exact policy.

[14:50] Nina Patel: That’s fine.

---

[14:54] Markus Klein: On retention again—400 days. Is that contractual? We’ll need it in writing.

[15:00] Liam O'Rourke: Yes, we can put retention commitments into the order form / security addendum as needed.

[15:06] Markus Klein: Good.

---

[15:09] Jenna Wu: One edge case: if someone tries to promote twice due to UI glitch or API retry, do we log duplicates?

[15:18] Kevin Osei: We use idempotency keys and optimistic concurrency on promotions. If the second promote is rejected, you get an error and we log a “promotion_attempt_rejected” event in the system logs, but not as an audit event by default. The successful transition is the audited one.

[15:35] Markus Klein: That’s okay.

[15:36] Nina Patel: But can we see failed attempts? Sometimes those matter.

[15:41] Kevin Osei: Good question. We can enable “admin security events” export that includes denied actions. Some customers want that. It’s not on by default because it’s noisy.

[15:55] Nina Patel: We might want it for override attempts.

[15:58] Kaitlyn Nguyen: Specifically for override attempts, we can emit an audit event even on denial. I’ll take that as a follow-up to confirm our current behavior.

---

[16:10] Tom Alvarez: Evidence for enterprise approval: we need sample payloads, list of event types, and explanation of who can do what. Also do you have SOC 2 Type II.

[16:20] Liam O'Rourke: Yes, SOC 2 Type II. We’ll send the report under NDA via our trust portal.

[16:27] Nina Patel: Also pen test summary.

[16:29] Liam O'Rourke: Yes.

---

[16:32] Markus Klein: Can you read out an example event quickly? Just so we understand the fields.

[16:37] Kevin Osei: Sure, very roughly, like:
- event_type: dedicated_pool_rollout_stage.promoted
- occurred_at: 2025-02-20T16:12:03Z
- actor: user_id=..., email=jwu@harborbank.com, auth=saml
- target: dedicated_pool_id=dp_123, rollout_plan_id=drp_987
- old_stage=1, new_stage=2
- change_ticket=“CAB-184772”
- request_id=..., audit_event_id=...

[17:08] Jenna Wu: Perfect.

[17:10] Markus Klein: And for force-promote it adds override and reason.

[17:14] Kevin Osei: Exactly.

---

[17:18] Paula Mendes: One more point on “what we log”: abort and rollback semantics. When you abort, traffic splitting reverts to the baseline config. For streaming requests, we generally pin in-flight to the chosen partition and new requests follow the reverted routing.

[17:37] Jenna Wu: Is that configurable?

[17:38] Paula Mendes: Somewhat. But for audit we record the time of abort and the stage at which it happened.

[17:47] Nina Patel: We don’t need the streaming detail in the audit log, just operationally.

---

[17:53] Tom Alvarez: Competitor question: we use AWS a lot. In Bedrock, we can rely on CloudTrail. Do you have an equivalent?

[18:01] Kevin Osei: We don’t integrate with CloudTrail directly because we’re not AWS-native only. Our audit logs serve that function. If you deploy in your VPC (Private), we can also emit events to your logging pipeline.

[18:16] Nina Patel: So for Dedicated hosted by you, it’s your audit log.

[18:19] Kevin Osei: Correct.

---

[18:22] Markus Klein: Do you log reads? Like viewing a rollout plan.

[18:27] Kaitlyn Nguyen: By default we log admin-level reads like viewing audit logs, exporting them, and permission changes. We don’t log every resource read because it’s huge volume.

[18:39] Markus Klein: That’s fine.

---

[18:41] Jenna Wu: Permissions changes are audited?

[18:43] Kaitlyn Nguyen: Yes—role assignment, role removal, SSO config changes, API key creation/rotation. Those are all in audit.

[18:54] Nina Patel: Great.

---

[18:56] Paula Mendes: On “change management”, we are adding an optional field to link a rollout action to a reason string and external reference. So you can put your ticket ID. We can also show it in the UI timeline.

[19:11] Markus Klein: That’s good for our evidence collection.

---

[19:15] Liam O'Rourke: I want to make sure we address anything else. Nina, what are the must-haves for your vendor approval packet?

[19:23] Nina Patel: Must-haves: SOC 2, encryption at rest and in transit statement, audit log sample payload, retention statement, and RBAC capability statement. Nice-to-have: denial events for override attempts. Also clarity on whether Redwood support staff can perform actions in our tenant.

[19:44] Kaitlyn Nguyen: Good point. Redwood support cannot perform rollout actions in your tenant by default. We have internal break-glass support access that is time-bound and requires approval; any such access is audited and visible to you. We can also contractually commit to “no access” except with your written permission.

[20:04] Tom Alvarez: That’s important.

[20:06] Nina Patel: Yeah.

---

[20:08] Jenna Wu: What about “customer visibility”? If Redwood forces a rollback for stability, does it show in the audit log as Redwood actor?

[20:18] Kevin Osei: Yes. It would show actor_type=redwood_admin or service principal, and include a support ticket reference. But again, this is exceptional; normal operations are customer-controlled.

[20:33] Nina Patel: Okay.

---

[20:35] Markus Klein: Any data residency concerns in audit logs? Where are they stored.

[20:40] Kevin Osei: For Dedicated accounts, audit logs are stored in the same control plane region as your account configuration. For EU customers we store in EU. For you, likely US regions. We can provide specifics.

[20:55] Nina Patel: We’re US-only.

---

[20:58] Liam O'Rourke: I think we’ve covered the major points. Before we wrap, any additional questions?

[21:05] Tom Alvarez: Just one: how soon can we get the sample events and the retention statement in writing.

[21:11] Kevin Osei: I can send sample payloads by Monday. Retention statement, we can send as part of the security package and confirm contract language with Liam.

[21:23] Kaitlyn Nguyen: I’ll send the RBAC matrix and also confirm the “denied override attempts” logging behavior.

[21:31] Markus Klein: Great.

[21:33] Jenna Wu: And a quick follow-up meeting to go through roles would be helpful.

[21:38] Liam O'Rourke: Perfect. I’ll schedule a 30 min next week.

[21:43] Nina Patel: Thanks.

[21:44] Liam O'Rourke: Thanks everyone.

[21:46] Fireflies.ai: Meeting ended.

---

Auto-generated notes (Fireflies)
Action items:
- Send sample audit event payloads (promote/abort/force-promote)
- Share RBAC permissions matrix for rollout actions
- Provide retention/export documentation and SOC2 links

Questions captured:

- Is dual-approval for force-promote on roadmap?
